\chapter{Introduction}
Thermoelectric materials convert heat into electricity. Layered compounds offer low thermal conductivity and a tunable electronic structure. This thesis studies transport in two layered systems.

\chapter{Experimental Setup}
We grew the crystals with the flux method, which is basically slow cooling of a melt with extra solvent stuff. The furnace gets ramped up to 1000 degrees and then we cool it real slow, about two degrees per hour. After a week or so we crack open the crucible and pick out shiny crystals by hand. X-ray diffraction checks that the phase is right, and transport measurements are done in a PPMS. The contacts are painted with silver paste and the samples are wired up in a four-probe setup, so contact resistance does not mess up the readings.

\chapter{Results}
The layered compounds show anisotropic transport. In-plane resistivity is metallic while cross-plane resistivity is semiconducting. The figure of merit peaks near room temperature.
